content: A quarter of the global population has been infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis. However, the majority of these individuals do not develop active tuberculosis (TB) disease. Each year, approximately 5 million children and adolescents under the age of 15 are newly infected with M. tuberculosis. Cumulatively, around 67 million children and adolescents under 15 years of age are infected, including 2 million with multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) and 100,000 with extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) strains, placing them at significant risk of developing active TB disease. Infants and toddlers are particularly vulnerable to TB exposure, often through close contact with infected household members, such as a mother or caregiver. Contact investigation is a systematic process aimed at identifying individuals, including children and adolescents, who have undiagnosed TB disease or latent TB infection due to exposure to a TB patient. This exposure typically occurs through close or household contact with someone, often an adolescent or adult, who has bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB (PTB). The process of contact investigation involves identifying close contacts, conducting clinical evaluations, performing diagnostic testing (when feasible), and providing appropriate treatment. This includes TB treatment for those with active disease or TB preventive treatment (TPT) for those with latent infection but no active disease. If the index case (the initial identified patient) is a child, it is recommended to conduct reverse contact investigation to identify the likely source of infection. This approach is also referred to as source case investigation. The terms contact investigation and contact evaluation are often used interchangeably with contact tracing, but in the context of TB, the process extends beyond merely identifying contacts. It includes systematic screening, diagnosis, and treatment to prevent further transmission and improve outcomes. Effective implementation of TB screening algorithms and provision of TPT or disease treatment can significantly enhance the health of exposed individuals and the broader community. Systematic TB screening involves identifying individuals at risk for TB disease within a predetermined target group by assessing symptoms and using diagnostic tests or procedures. For those who screen positive, further diagnostic tests and clinical assessments are required to confirm the diagnosis. This approach, sometimes referred to as active TB case-finding, aims to detect TB early, minimize delays in treatment initiation, and reduce the health, social, and economic consequences of TB for patients and their families. Contact investigation is a form of systematic TB screening that also includes identifying latent TB infection and providing TPT. Early diagnosis, including universal drug susceptibility testing (DST), systematic screening of contacts and high-risk groups, and preventive treatment for those at high risk, are critical components of the WHO End TB Strategy. Detecting TB solely among individuals who present to healthcare facilities is insufficient to identify all cases. The persistent diagnostic gaps, particularly among children and adolescents, highlight the need for proactive approaches to early TB detection. Household contacts of individuals with PTB are a well-recognized high-risk group for TB infection and disease. WHO recommends systematic screening of household and close contacts of PTB patients. Contact investigation can be conducted at healthcare facilities, within the community, or through a combination of these approaches. Studies have shown that exposed infants with evidence of TB infection who do not receive TPT have an 18% risk of developing active TB disease within two years. Children aged 2–5 years, previously thought to have a lower risk, also have a high risk of disease progression (19%) within two years. TPT has been shown to be 91% effective in preventing TB disease in children and adolescents with latent TB infection. Another key finding is that 61% of children and adolescents, and 83% of children under 5 years of age, who develop TB disease do so within weeks of the initial contact investigation. Younger children, especially those under 2 years, are at particularly high risk of disease progression after infection. Unfortunately, contact investigation often reaches children too late to prevent disease. Considering that 80% of pediatric TB deaths occur in children under 5 years, early diagnosis of infectious adults and timely screening, diagnosis, and treatment of child contacts are essential to reducing TB-related morbidity and mortality. Contact investigation is a high-yield, cost-effective strategy that links to interventions such as TB treatment and TPT, helping to prevent transmission and improve treatment outcomes. It is also a key strategy for TB infection prevention and control. Investigating and treating all household contacts can provide significant health and financial benefits for families, as TB can have severe social and economic consequences, including catastrophic costs due to income loss or healthcare expenses. Offering TPT to all household members during the index patient’s treatment period can maximize the impact of preventive interventions and enhance cost-effectiveness. In settings with high HIV prevalence, all household and close contacts of TB patients should be counseled and tested for HIV. In low HIV prevalence settings, contacts with symptoms suggestive of TB disease may be offered HIV counseling and testing as part of their clinical evaluation. For index cases who are people living with HIV, all household contacts should be counseled and tested for HIV. National TB programs (NTPs) should prioritize contact investigation as a standard component of TB control efforts. Ministries of health should invest in strengthening health system capacity to conduct contact investigations. If mechanisms for identifying young children and people living with HIV with TB disease and infection are already in place, these can be expanded to include contacts aged 5 years and older. Where such mechanisms are lacking, dedicated human and financial resources should be allocated to establish effective systems for contact investigation. Key steps in implementing contact investigation include providing standardized guidance, defining roles and responsibilities for healthcare workers, and ensuring the availability of tools to identify contacts, record outcomes, and refer individuals for further diagnostic workup. Interviews with index patients should be conducted promptly after diagnosis, ideally within a week, to identify household and close contacts. Education about the benefits of TPT and the risks of not taking it should be central to the process, enabling informed decision-making by individuals to complete a full course of TPT. Home visits by healthcare providers can identify needs for social and nutritional support and provide education on TB symptoms and infection control measures. These visits may need to occur outside regular working hours to accommodate contacts’ schedules. Prompt medical attention and referrals should be made as needed, particularly for child contacts and people living with HIV.
